records.name: Direct Callback Coupling
records.definition: Wiring a source to notify specific recipients by direct call, coupling it to each one.

records.name: Direct Method Invocation
records.definition: Invoking an operation by direct method call, so it cannot be queued, logged, or undone.

records.name: Duplicated Workflow
records.definition: Repeating the same overall algorithm in many places, each copy re-implementing the shared steps.

records.name: Exposed Internal Representation
records.definition: Forcing clients to traverse a collection through its internal structure, coupling them to that structure.

records.name: External State Reach-In
records.definition: Reading or writing an object's internal state from outside to snapshot it, breaking its encapsulation.

records.name: Flat State Explosion
records.definition: Enumerating every combination of conditions as a separate flat state, so the state count explodes.

records.name: Large Conditional Logic
records.definition: Selecting behavior with a large branching conditional instead of pluggable strategy objects.

records.name: Mesh Dependencies
records.definition: Letting every object refer directly to every other, forming a dense mesh of point-to-point dependencies.

records.name: Monolithic Handler
records.definition: Handling every case in one large handler instead of a chain of focused, single-purpose handlers.

records.name: Centralized Interaction Logic
records.definition: The ability to concentrate how a set of objects interact within one mediating component.

records.name: Controlled Variation
records.definition: The ability to let subclasses vary only the designated steps of a fixed algorithm.

records.name: Decoupled Notification
records.definition: The ability to notify interested parties of a change without the source knowing who they are.

records.name: Deferred Execution
records.definition: The ability to capture a request as an object so it can be run later, held in a queue, or logged.

records.name: Exhaustive State Reasoning
records.definition: The ability to enumerate and reason about every state a system can occupy and every transition between them.

records.name: Framework Reuse
records.definition: The ability to reuse a fixed algorithm skeleton across many concrete implementations.

records.name: Guarded Transitions
records.definition: The ability to permit a state transition only when a specified condition holds.

records.name: Hierarchical States

distinctFrom.reason: Hierarchical states nest states to share behavior, while guarded transitions condition a move between states.
Hierarchical states nest one state inside another, while parallel regions run independent states at the same time.

records.definition: The ability to nest states so shared behavior is defined once on an enclosing state.

records.name: Lazy Traversal
records.definition: The ability to produce a collection's elements one at a time on demand rather than all at once.

records.name: Null-Check Elimination
records.definition: The ability to remove scattered null checks by substituting a benign do-nothing object.

records.name: Operation Extension Without Element Change
records.definition: The ability to add new operations over a structure without modifying its element classes.

records.name: Ordered Fallthrough
records.definition: The ability to offer a request to handlers in sequence until one of them accepts it.

records.name: Parallel Regions

distinctFrom.reason: Parallel regions are independent states active at once, while guarded transitions condition one move between states.

records.definition: The ability to model concurrently-active, independent regions of state within one machine.

records.name: Pluggable Handling

distinctFrom.reason: Pluggable handling adds or reorders handlers without changing the others, while ordered fallthrough offers a request to each handler in turn until one accepts.

records.definition: The ability to add or reorder request handlers without changing the ones already in the chain.

records.name: Runtime Behavior Selection
records.definition: The ability to choose among interchangeable algorithms at runtime.

records.name: Snapshot/Restore
records.definition: The ability to capture an object's state and later restore it to that captured point.

records.name: State-Local Behavior
records.definition: The ability to attach behavior to each state so an object acts according to its current state.

records.name: Structure-Agnostic Iteration

distinctFrom.reason: Structure-agnostic iteration hides how a collection is organized, while lazy traversal produces its elements only on demand.

records.definition: The ability to traverse a collection without depending on how it is internally organized.

records.name: Fail-Safe Defaults
records.definition: Defaulting to safe, benign behavior when a value or handler is absent rather than failing or branching.

records.name: Explicit State Model
records.definition: The requirement that an object's states and their transitions be modeled explicitly.

records.name: Explicit State Set
records.definition: The requirement that the complete set of possible states be defined up front.

records.name: Interchangeable Algorithms
records.definition: The requirement that competing algorithms share one interface so they can be swapped freely.

records.name: Shared Behavioral Interface
records.definition: The requirement that the real object and its null stand-in implement one common interface.

records.name: Stable Algorithm Skeleton
records.definition: The requirement that the overall algorithm's structure stay fixed while specific steps vary.

records.name: Stable Element Hierarchy
records.definition: The requirement that the set of element types stay fixed so new operations can be added over them.

records.name: Subject/Subscriber Contract
records.definition: The requirement of an agreed interface by which subjects notify and subscribers receive updates.

records.name: Uniform Handler Interface
records.definition: The requirement that every handler in a chain share one interface so requests pass along uniformly.

records.name: Uniform Traversal Interface
records.definition: The requirement that collections expose one common interface for stepping through their elements.

records.name: Class Count
records.definition: The degree to which extracting each algorithm into its own class raises the total number of classes.

records.name: Class Proliferation
records.definition: The degree to which modeling each state as its own class multiplies the number of classes.

records.name: Coordination Complexity
records.definition: The degree of complexity in how objects must coordinate, which motivates a mediator.

records.name: Element Stability
records.definition: The degree to which adding new operations stays easy only while the set of element types stays fixed.

records.name: Inheritance Coupling
records.definition: The degree to which basing a template method on subclassing binds subclasses tightly to the base class.

records.name: Mediator God Object
records.definition: The degree to which concentrating interaction logic in a mediator risks growing it into an overloaded object.

records.name: Memory Footprint
records.definition: The degree of memory consumed by retaining state snapshots for later restoration.

records.name: Silent No-Op Risk
records.definition: The degree to which a do-nothing stand-in can hide an error.

records.name: State Explosion
records.definition: The degree to which the number of explicit states grows unmanageably as conditions multiply.

records.name: Encode State Machine
records.definition: A technique for declaring the states and legal transitions of a lifecycle, so an operation called in the wrong state is refused.

records.name: Make Order Explicit
records.definition: A technique for expressing a required call order in types or a state machine instead of in documentation.

records.name: Scattered Null Guards
records.definition: A defect in which every call site repeats a null check before the same operation.
